title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Ypsilanti data center water and power debates amid today's court battles and Nessel appeals.

lines.text: Good evening and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy, the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Tonight we're zeroing in on a Ypsilanti data center proposal that puts water and power tradeoffs front and center, right as multiple communities take steps to hit pause.

That Ypsilanti story from yesterday really captures the tension, doesn't it? An EMU hydrogeologist talking about closed-loop cooling reusing groundwater without warming the subsurface, while an activist flags possible new energy infrastructure as a potential community plus.
Exactly. It shows how these projects aren't just about servers in a warehouse anymore.
So walk me through the bigger picture here. How did we get to this point where every new proposal seems to spark fights over rates, water, and local control?

It really accelerated this year as AI demand pushed developers toward Michigan's available land and power. Places like Washtenaw and Oakland counties started seeing applications that could pull hundreds of megawatts each.
And that scale means real impacts on the grid and aquifers, right?
Precisely. A single large facility can require new transmission upgrades that utilities want to recover through rates, and cooling often draws from groundwater or needs massive electricity.
What does that look like for regular ratepayers thirty miles away who never asked for this?
They could see higher electric bills if costs get spread across the system, plus shifts in local tax bases if incentives are offered to lure the projects.
And water? Is that the hidden piece people are waking up to?
It is. Closed-loop systems are pitched as more efficient, but even then there's extraction and potential strain on supplies, especially in areas already watching drought trends.
The Ypsilanti discussion mentioned benefits like new infrastructure too. Is that the trade-off communities are weighing?
Some officials see tax revenue and jobs, but others worry the infrastructure upgrades mainly serve the data center and leave residents footing part of the bill.
How many places are actually moving to slow things down right now?
Quite a few. Oakland County has a suburb with a temporary freeze facing a lawsuit today from a developer. Lowell Township in Kent County is drafting rules on size, noise, and power use.
And that's after similar pushes in other townships this week.
Yes, and it ties directly into what Attorney General Nessel is doing on the power side.
She's appealing that DTE deal for the Saline data center, correct?
Filed opening arguments today challenging how costs get allocated for that massive new load.
And separately she's pushing the PSC to block utilities from shifting infrastructure costs onto regular customers.
That's the core of it. She wants stronger oversight so residents aren't subsidizing these big tech projects through their monthly bills.
What happens if the court sides with the developer in Oakland or the appeal fails?
It could set precedents that make it harder for towns to pause projects or force utilities to absorb more of the upgrade costs themselves.
Or easier for them to spread costs statewide.
Exactly, which is why these cases are being watched far beyond the immediate sites.
Any sense of timeline on the Ypsilanti project itself?
Still early, but the comments from the hydrogeologist and activist suggest the planning commission is digging into the technical details before any approvals.
And meanwhile Mason County is questioning whether its grid can even handle a surge from proposed AI facilities.
Western Michigan utilities are flagging transmission constraints and asking who pays for upgrades or new plants.
That feels like the same conversation playing out in multiple counties at once.
It is. A state senator also warned local officials this week about rate spikes and water strain if rules aren't tightened.
So what's the next step for communities trying to get ahead of applications?
Drafting ordinances like the ones Lowell and West Michigan townships are reviewing, plus pushing the PSC for clearer cost allocation rules.
And Nessel's pressure on the commission could influence that.
Her demands for answers on how surging demand is handled signal growing pushback at the state level too.
Alright, let's shift to a few other developments from today and yesterday in our quick hits.
First up, that Oakland County lawsuit filed today. A developer is challenging a suburb's six-month freeze on new data centers.
The case tests how much local governments can pause these power-hungry projects before court intervention.
Residents even thirty miles away could feel it through rates or tax base changes depending on the ruling.
Next, Attorney General Nessel and environmental groups filed arguments today appealing the DTE contract for the Saline data center.
The fight is over whether the rate structure fairly spreads costs for that huge new demand.
If it stands, local bills could rise. Nessel is also pressing the PSC separately to stop utilities from passing data center costs to everyone else.
That Michigan Advance roundup this week pulled together all the active tax break, grid, and water fights happening simultaneously.
It shows how one project's incentives can ripple to ratepayers far from the site.
Yesterday Lowell Township's planning commission moved forward with a new ordinance targeting data center size, noise, and power demands.
Aiming to avoid the heavy electricity and water issues seen elsewhere in the state.
West Michigan officials also got their first detailed look at how these facilities could affect roads, noise, and electric demand in their area.
They're drafting rules proactively before any applications land.
And a state senator flagged the risks to suburbs around Detroit and beyond if local rules stay weak.
Now let's look at the meetings listeners can attend starting tonight.
Rochester Hills City Council meets today to vote on extending its six-month data center moratorium by another 180 days.
London Township Board of Trustees is taking up its data center ordinance this evening as well.
Morley Village has a public hearing on a proposed data center project.
Lowell Charter Township Planning Commission will discuss its data center ordinance and moratorium proposal tonight.
And tomorrow Lowell Township Planning Commission follows up with its own ordinance proposal.
Plenty of chances for residents to weigh in directly.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.
Thanks for listening.

episode_title: Ypsilanti Plan Spotlights Water-Power Tradeoffs as Moratoriums and Rate Fights Spread
